text: State the law of conservation of mass and the law of definite proportions.
modelAnswer: Law of conservation of mass: in a chemical reaction matter is neither created nor destroyed, so the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. Law of definite proportions: a given chemical compound always contains the same elements combined in the same fixed ratio by mass, whatever its source or method of preparation.
keyPoints: Mass of reactants = mass of products
Fixed mass ratio of elements in a compound

text: Distinguish between molarity and molality. Which one is preferred for work at varying temperatures and why?
modelAnswer: Molarity (M) = moles of solute per litre of solution. Molality (m) = moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. Molality is preferred because it uses masses, which do not change with temperature. Molarity uses volume, which expands or contracts as the temperature changes.

text: A compound contains 40.0% C, 6.67% H and 53.33% O by mass. Its molar mass is 60 g mol⁻¹. Find its empirical and molecular formulae.
modelAnswer: Take 100 g of compound. Moles: C = 40.0/12 = 3.33; H = 6.67/1 = 6.67; O = 53.33/16 = 3.33. Divide by the smallest (3.33): C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1, so the empirical formula is CH₂O (mass 30 g mol⁻¹). n = 60/30 = 2, so the molecular formula is C₂H₄O₂.

text: Calculate the molarity and molality of a solution made by dissolving 4 g of NaOH in 250 g of water. Assume the density of the solution is 1.0 g mL⁻¹.
modelAnswer: Moles of NaOH = 4/40 = 0.1 mol. Molality = 0.1 mol ÷ 0.250 kg = 0.4 mol kg⁻¹. Mass of solution = 250 + 4 = 254 g, so with density 1.0 g mL⁻¹ the volume = 254 mL = 0.254 L. Molarity = 0.1/0.254 = 0.394 mol L⁻¹ (about 0.39 M).
keyPoints: Solution volume = 254 mL from mass and density

text: (a) What is a limiting reagent? (b) 50.0 kg of N₂ and 10.0 kg of H₂ are mixed to make ammonia: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Identify the limiting reagent and calculate the mass of NH₃ formed. Also find the mass of the reagent left unreacted.
modelAnswer:
(a) The limiting reagent is the reactant that is used up first. It fixes how much product can form; the other reactants are left in excess.
(b) n(N₂) = 50 000/28 = 1785.7 mol; n(H₂) = 10 000/2 = 5000 mol. To react all the N₂ we would need 3 × 1785.7 = 5357 mol of H₂, but only 5000 mol is present, so H₂ is the limiting reagent.
NH₃ formed = (2/3) × 5000 = 3333.3 mol = 3333.3 × 17 = 56 667 g ≈ 56.7 kg.
N₂ used = 5000/3 = 1666.7 mol = 46.67 kg, so N₂ left = 50.0 − 46.67 = 3.33 kg.

text: Calculate the number of moles and the number of molecules present in 3.42 g of sucrose (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁, molar mass 342 g mol⁻¹).
modelAnswer: n = 3.42 g ÷ 342 g mol⁻¹ = 0.01 mol. Number of molecules = 0.01 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 6.022 × 10²¹.

text: State Heisenberg's uncertainty principle. Why is it not significant for macroscopic objects?
modelAnswer: Heisenberg's principle: it is impossible to determine the exact position and the exact momentum of a microscopic particle at the same time, Δx · Δp ≥ h/4π. For macroscopic objects the mass is very large, so the uncertainty in velocity (Δv = h/4πmΔx) is far too small to measure and has no practical effect.
keyPoints: Simultaneous exact position and momentum impossible

text: Write the four quantum numbers and state what each describes. Give all the allowed sets of n, l, mₗ for n = 2.
modelAnswer:
Principal quantum number n (1, 2, 3, …) gives the shell, its size and its energy. Azimuthal quantum number l (0 to n − 1) gives the subshell and the shape of the orbital (s, p, d, f). Magnetic quantum number mₗ (−l to +l) gives the orientation of the orbital in space. Spin quantum number mₛ (+½ or −½) gives the spin of the electron.
For n = 2: (2, 0, 0) for the 2s orbital; (2, 1, −1), (2, 1, 0), (2, 1, +1) for the three 2p orbitals. That is 4 orbitals, holding 8 electrons.

text: Calculate the frequency and wavelength of the radiation emitted when the electron in a hydrogen atom falls from n = 4 to n = 2. (R_H = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
keyPoints: Correct Rydberg expression with n₁ = 2, n₂ = 4

text: Write the electronic configurations of Cu (Z = 29) and Cu²⁺. Why is the configuration of Cu an exception?
modelAnswer: Cu: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, i.e. [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. Cu²⁺: [Ar] 3d⁹. The Aufbau order would predict 3d⁹ 4s², but a completely filled 3d¹⁰ subshell is extra stable, because of its symmetrical distribution and greater exchange energy. So one 4s electron moves into 3d.

text: (a) State the postulates of Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom. (b) Give two limitations of the model. (c) Calculate the energy required to remove the electron from the n = 2 orbit of a hydrogen atom, in joules (E₁ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J).
modelAnswer:
(a) (i) The electron revolves around the nucleus in certain fixed circular orbits (stationary states) without radiating energy. (ii) Only orbits in which the angular momentum is a whole-number multiple of h/2π are allowed: mvr = nh/2π. (iii) Energy is absorbed or emitted only when the electron jumps between orbits, and ΔE = E₂ − E₁ = hν.
(b) It cannot explain the spectra of multi-electron atoms. It cannot explain the splitting of lines in magnetic and electric fields (Zeeman and Stark effects). It also conflicts with de Broglie's dual nature and Heisenberg's principle, because it assigns exact orbits.
(c) E₂ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸/2² = −5.45 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Energy to remove the electron (n = 2 → ∞) = 0 − (−5.45 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 5.45 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per atom.

text: Draw (or describe) the shapes of the s, p and d_z² orbitals and state the number of angular nodes in each.
modelAnswer: s orbital: spherical, 0 angular nodes. p orbital: dumb-bell shaped, two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus with a nodal plane between them, 1 angular node. d_z²: a dumb-bell along the z-axis with a doughnut-shaped ring (collar) in the xy-plane, 2 angular nodes (here they are two conical surfaces).

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
text: State the modern periodic law. How did it remove the anomaly of the position of argon and potassium in Mendeleev's table?
modelAnswer: Modern periodic law: the physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers. Argon (Ar, 39.9) is heavier than potassium (K, 39.1), so a mass-based order would put K before Ar. By atomic number, Ar (18) comes before K (19), so both fall naturally into the correct groups: Ar with the noble gases and K with the alkali metals.
keyPoints: Order by Z places each in its correct group

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
text: Explain why the first ionisation enthalpy (a) decreases down a group, (b) of Be is greater than that of B, and (c) of Mg is greater than that of Al.
modelAnswer:
(a) Down a group a new shell is added at each step, so the atomic radius increases and the inner electrons shield the valence electron more. The outer electron is held less strongly, so ionisation enthalpy falls.
(b) Be (2s²) loses an electron from the penetrating 2s orbital, which is held more strongly. B (2s² 2p¹) loses a 2p electron, which is shielded by the 2s electrons and held less tightly.
(c) In the same way, Mg (3s²) has a filled 3s subshell, while Al loses its single 3p electron, which is easier to remove.
keyPoints: Size and shielding increase down a group
s electron more penetrating than p
Filled s² subshell more stable than s² p¹

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
text: What is electron gain enthalpy? Why is the electron gain enthalpy of fluorine less negative than that of chlorine?
modelAnswer: Electron gain enthalpy (ΔegH) is the enthalpy change when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom: X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g). It is negative when energy is released. Fluorine is very small, so its 2p subshell is compact. An incoming electron feels strong repulsion from the electrons already there. In chlorine the added electron enters the larger 3p subshell, where there is less repulsion. So more energy is released, and ΔegH of Cl (−349 kJ mol⁻¹) is more negative than that of F (−328 kJ mol⁻¹).

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
text: How would you predict the block, period and group of an element with Z = 20?
modelAnswer: Configuration: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s². The last electron enters an s orbital, so it is an s-block element. The highest principal quantum number is 4, so it is in period 4. With 2 valence electrons in an s-block element, it is in Group 2 (calcium).

chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
text: Discuss the trends in (a) atomic radius, (b) ionisation enthalpy, (c) electronegativity and (d) metallic character across a period and down a group. Explain each in terms of effective nuclear charge and shell number.
modelAnswer:
(a) Atomic radius decreases across a period: the effective nuclear charge (Z_eff) increases while electrons enter the same shell. It increases down a group because a new shell is added each time.
(b) Ionisation enthalpy generally increases across a period (higher Z_eff, smaller atom; small dips at Group 13 and Group 16 because of subshell effects). It decreases down a group (larger size, more shielding).
(c) Electronegativity increases across a period (greater pull on bonding electrons by a smaller, more highly charged atom) and decreases down a group.
(d) Metallic character (the tendency to lose electrons) decreases across a period and increases down a group. This follows the ionisation enthalpy trend in reverse.
Overall: a higher Z_eff and fewer shells mean electrons are held more tightly.
keyPoints: Explained via Z_eff and shell number

text: What is hybridisation? Give the hybridisation and shape for BeCl₂ and SF₆.
modelAnswer: Hybridisation is the mixing of atomic orbitals of slightly different energies on the same atom to form an equal number of new, equivalent hybrid orbitals of identical shape and energy. BeCl₂ is sp hybridised and linear (180°). SF₆ is sp³d² hybridised and octahedral (90°).
keyPoints: Definition: mixing of orbitals of similar energy into equivalent hybrids

text: Using VSEPR theory, predict the shapes of (a) NH₃, (b) H₂O, (c) XeF₂. Give the number of bond pairs and lone pairs in each.
modelAnswer:
(a) NH₃: 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair (4 electron pairs, sp³). The shape is trigonal pyramidal, angle about 107°.
(b) H₂O: 2 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs (sp³). The shape is bent (V-shaped), angle about 104.5°.
(c) XeF₂: 2 bond pairs + 3 lone pairs (5 electron pairs, sp³d). The three lone pairs take the equatorial positions, so the molecule is linear (180°).

text: Draw the molecular orbital energy-level diagram for O₂. Write its MO configuration, calculate its bond order and explain its magnetic behaviour. Compare the bond orders and bond lengths of O₂⁺, O₂ and O₂⁻.
modelAnswer:
O₂ has 16 electrons. For O₂ and F₂, σ2p lies below π2p. MO configuration: KK (σ2s)² (σ*2s)² (σ2p_z)² (π2p_x)² (π2p_y)² (π*2p_x)¹ (π*2p_y)¹.
Bonding electrons (valence) N_b = 8; antibonding electrons N_a = 4. Bond order = (8 − 4)/2 = 2.
The two π* electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins (Hund's rule), so O₂ is paramagnetic. Valence bond theory cannot explain this.
O₂⁺ (one fewer π* electron): BO = 2.5. O₂⁻ (one more π* electron): BO = 1.5. A higher bond order means a shorter, stronger bond, so bond length: O₂⁺ < O₂ < O₂⁻. All three are paramagnetic.
keyPoints: Correct MO filling with σ2p below π2p for O₂
Bond length inversely related to bond order

text: State Fajans' rules. Explain why AgCl is less soluble in water than NaCl although Ag⁺ and Na⁺ are of similar size.
modelAnswer:
Fajans' rules: an ionic bond acquires more covalent character when (i) the cation is small, (ii) the charge on either ion is high, (iii) the anion is large (easily polarised), and (iv) the cation has a pseudo-noble-gas (18-electron, ns² np⁶ nd¹⁰) configuration rather than a noble-gas one.
Ag⁺ has an 18-electron shell (4d¹⁰). d electrons shield the nucleus poorly, so Ag⁺ is much more polarising than Na⁺ (an 8-electron shell). It distorts the Cl⁻ cloud and gives AgCl substantial covalent character, so AgCl is far less soluble in polar water.
keyPoints: Small cation, high charge, large anion favour covalency
AgCl partly covalent → low solubility in water

text: Define dipole moment and give its unit. Why is BF₃ non-polar although the B–F bond is polar?
modelAnswer: Dipole moment μ = charge × distance of separation (q × d). It is a vector, measured in debye (1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m). BF₃ is trigonal planar with three equal B–F bond dipoles at 120°, so their vector sum is zero and the net dipole moment is zero.
keyPoints: Symmetrical trigonal planar shape cancels bond dipoles

text: What is a hydrogen bond? Explain why ice floats on water.
modelAnswer: A hydrogen bond is a weak electrostatic attraction between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom (F, O or N) and a lone pair on another such atom. In ice, each water molecule is hydrogen-bonded tetrahedrally to four others, forming an open, cage-like structure with large empty spaces. So ice is less dense than liquid water and floats.
keyPoints: H bonded to F/O/N attracted to lone pair

chapter: States of Matter: Gases and Liquids
text: State Dalton's law of partial pressures and write its mathematical form. What is aqueous tension?
modelAnswer: Dalton's law: the total pressure of a mixture of non-reacting gases equals the sum of the partial pressures of its components, P_total = p₁ + p₂ + p₃ + …, where pᵢ = xᵢ × P_total. When a gas is collected over water it is saturated with water vapour. The pressure due to this water vapour at that temperature is the aqueous tension, so p(dry gas) = P_total − aqueous tension.
keyPoints: Aqueous tension = vapour pressure of water; subtract it

chapter: States of Matter: Gases and Liquids
text: Calculate the volume occupied by 8.8 g of CO₂ at 27 °C and 1 atm pressure. (R = 0.0821 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

chapter: States of Matter: Gases and Liquids
text: State Graham's law of diffusion. 50 mL of hydrogen diffuses through a pinhole in 20 s. How long will 40 mL of oxygen take to diffuse through the same hole under the same conditions?
modelAnswer:
Graham's law: at the same temperature and pressure, the rate of diffusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its density (or molar mass): r ∝ 1/√M.
r(H₂) = 50/20 = 2.5 mL s⁻¹. r(O₂) = r(H₂) × √(2/32) = 2.5 × 0.25 = 0.625 mL s⁻¹.
Time for 40 mL O₂ = 40/0.625 = 64 s.

chapter: States of Matter: Gases and Liquids
text: (a) Why do real gases deviate from ideal behaviour? Name the two faulty assumptions of kinetic theory. (b) Write the van der Waals equation for n moles and explain the corrections. (c) Define compressibility factor Z and explain what Z > 1 and Z < 1 indicate. (d) Under what conditions do real gases behave ideally?
modelAnswer:
(a) Kinetic theory assumes that (i) gas molecules have negligible volume compared with the container and (ii) there are no forces of attraction between them. At high pressure the molecular volume becomes significant, and at low temperature attractions become significant, so both assumptions fail.
(b) (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT. Pressure correction an²/V²: attractions from the bulk pull back molecules about to hit the wall, so the observed P is less than the ideal value and must be increased. Volume correction nb: the molecules occupy volume, so the free space is V − nb (b ≈ 4 × the actual volume of 1 mol of molecules).
(c) Z = PV/nRT (= 1 for an ideal gas). Z > 1: repulsions dominate and the gas is harder to compress (e.g. H₂, He, or any gas at very high P). Z < 1: attractions dominate and the gas is easier to compress (e.g. CO₂, NH₃ at moderate P).
(d) At low pressure and high temperature (especially above the Boyle temperature), real gases behave nearly ideally.
keyPoints: Two faulty assumptions: negligible volume, no attraction
Meaning of a and b corrections
Ideal at low P, high T

chapter: States of Matter: Gases and Liquids
text: What are critical temperature and critical pressure? Why cannot CO₂ be liquefied at 40 °C, however high the pressure?
modelAnswer: Critical temperature (T_c): the temperature above which a gas cannot be liquefied, however much pressure is applied. Critical pressure (P_c): the minimum pressure needed to liquefy the gas at T_c. For CO₂, T_c ≈ 31 °C (304 K). At 40 °C the molecules have too much kinetic energy for the attractions to hold them in the liquid state, so pressure alone cannot liquefy it.

chapter: States of Matter: Gases and Liquids
text: Define surface tension and give one everyday consequence of it.
modelAnswer: Surface tension is the force acting per unit length perpendicular to a line drawn on the surface of a liquid (unit N m⁻¹). It arises because molecules at the surface feel a net inward pull. Because of it, liquid drops are spherical (a sphere has minimum surface area for a given volume). Other consequences: liquids rise in capillary tubes, and small insects can walk on water.
keyPoints: Force per unit length, N m⁻¹
Net inward pull on surface molecules

text: State the first law of thermodynamics and write its mathematical form. What are the IUPAC sign conventions for q and w?
modelAnswer: First law: energy can neither be created nor destroyed. The energy of an isolated system is constant. Mathematically ΔU = q + w. Sign convention: q is positive when heat is absorbed by the system and negative when released. w is positive when work is done on the system and negative when work is done by the system.
keyPoints: q +ve absorbed; w +ve done on system

text: Derive the relation ΔH = ΔU + Δn(g)RT. Calculate ΔH − ΔU for the combustion of ethanol at 298 K: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l).
modelAnswer:
H = U + PV, so at constant pressure ΔH = ΔU + PΔV. For ideal gases PV = nRT, so PΔV = Δn(g)RT. Hence ΔH = ΔU + Δn(g)RT, where Δn(g) = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants.
For ethanol combustion: Δn(g) = 2 − 3 = −1 (liquids are ignored).
ΔH − ΔU = −1 × 8.314 × 298 = −2478 J ≈ −2.48 kJ mol⁻¹.

text: The enthalpies of combustion of C(graphite), H₂(g) and CH₄(g) are −393.5, −285.8 and −890.3 kJ mol⁻¹ respectively. Calculate the enthalpy of formation of methane using Hess's law.
modelAnswer:
Target: C(s) + 2H₂(g) → CH₄(g).
(i) C + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −393.5
(ii) H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O(l), ΔH = −285.8; multiply by 2: −571.6
(iii) CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890.3; reverse it: +890.3
Add (i) + 2(ii) − (iii): ΔH°f(CH₄) = −393.5 − 571.6 + 890.3 = −74.8 kJ mol⁻¹.

text: (a) Define Gibbs energy and write the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation. (b) Using it, discuss the spontaneity of a reaction for all four combinations of signs of ΔH and ΔS. (c) For a reaction, ΔH = +40 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔG at 300 K and the temperature above which the reaction becomes spontaneous.
modelAnswer:
(a) Gibbs energy G = H − TS, a state function. At constant T and P, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. A process is spontaneous if ΔG < 0, at equilibrium if ΔG = 0 and non-spontaneous if ΔG > 0.
(b) (i) ΔH −, ΔS +: ΔG always negative, spontaneous at all T. (ii) ΔH +, ΔS −: ΔG always positive, never spontaneous. (iii) ΔH −, ΔS −: spontaneous at low T (when |ΔH| > |TΔS|). (iv) ΔH +, ΔS +: spontaneous at high T (when TΔS > ΔH).
(c) ΔG = 40 − 300 × 0.100 = 40 − 30 = +10 kJ mol⁻¹, so it is non-spontaneous at 300 K. T at which ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS = 40 000/100 = 400 K. The reaction is spontaneous above 400 K.
keyPoints: G = H − TS; ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
ΔG < 0 criterion at const T, P

text: Define (a) standard enthalpy of formation and (b) enthalpy of atomisation, with one example each.
modelAnswer:
(a) Standard enthalpy of formation (ΔH°f) is the enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound is formed from its elements in their most stable states under standard conditions (1 bar, usually 298 K). Example: C(graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH°f = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹.
(b) Enthalpy of atomisation (ΔaH) is the enthalpy change when 1 mol of bonds is broken completely to give gaseous atoms (or 1 mol of a substance is converted to gaseous atoms). Example: H₂(g) → 2H(g), ΔaH = +436 kJ mol⁻¹.
keyPoints: ΔH°f: 1 mol compound from elements in standard states

text: Why is the entropy of a substance at its gaseous state greater than in its liquid state? State the second law of thermodynamics in terms of entropy.
modelAnswer: Entropy measures the randomness (dispersal of energy and matter) of a system. Gas molecules move freely through a much larger volume and have many more possible arrangements (microstates) than in a liquid, so S(gas) > S(liquid). Second law: in any spontaneous process the total entropy of the universe (system + surroundings) increases: ΔS_total > 0.
keyPoints: Gas has greater freedom → higher S

text: State the law of mass action. Write the expression of K_c for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g).
modelAnswer: Law of mass action: at constant temperature, the rate of a reaction is proportional to the product of the molar concentrations of the reactants, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient. At equilibrium this gives a constant ratio. For the given reaction: K_c = [SO₃]² ÷ ([SO₂]² [O₂]).
keyPoints: Rate ∝ product of active masses with powers

text: State Le Chatelier's principle. Use it to predict the effect of (a) increasing pressure, (b) increasing temperature and (c) removing NH₃ on N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g); ΔH = −92 kJ.
modelAnswer:
Le Chatelier's principle: if a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure or temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that tends to undo the change.
(a) Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles (4 → 2), so it shifts forward and more NH₃ forms.
(b) The forward reaction is exothermic, so raising the temperature shifts it backward, decreasing the NH₃ yield (and K decreases).
(c) Removing NH₃ lowers the product concentration, so it shifts forward to make more NH₃.

text: Calculate the pH of a solution obtained by mixing 50 mL of 0.1 M HCl with 50 mL of 0.2 M NaOH.

(a) What is a buffer solution? Explain, with equations, how an acetic acid–sodium acetate buffer resists a change in pH on adding a small amount of acid or base. (b) Derive the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for an acidic buffer. (c) Calculate the pH of a buffer containing 0.2 M CH₃COOH and 0.1 M CH₃COONa (pK_a = 4.74).
modelAnswer:
(a) A buffer is a solution whose pH changes very little when a small amount of acid or base is added, or on dilution. In CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻ (from CH₃COONa): added H⁺ is removed by the acetate ion, CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH. Added OH⁻ is removed by the acid, CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O. So [H⁺] hardly changes.
(b) K_a = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA], so [H⁺] = K_a[HA]/[A⁻]. Taking −log: pH = pK_a + log([A⁻]/[HA]) = pK_a + log([salt]/[acid]), because the salt is fully ionised and the weak acid is barely ionised.
(c) pH = 4.74 + log(0.1/0.2) = 4.74 + log 0.5 = 4.74 − 0.30 = 4.44.
keyPoints: Equations for neutralising added H⁺ and OH⁻

text: The solubility product of Ag₂CrO₄ at 298 K is 1.1 × 10⁻¹². Calculate its molar solubility and the concentration of Ag⁺ in its saturated solution.
modelAnswer:
Ag₂CrO₄(s) ⇌ 2Ag⁺(aq) + CrO₄²⁻(aq). If the solubility is s, then [Ag⁺] = 2s and [CrO₄²⁻] = s.
K_sp = (2s)²(s) = 4s³ = 1.1 × 10⁻¹², so s³ = 2.75 × 10⁻¹³ and s = 6.5 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹.
[Ag⁺] = 2s = 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹.

text: Explain, with equations, why an aqueous solution of sodium carbonate is basic.
modelAnswer: Na₂CO₃ is the salt of a strong base (NaOH) and a weak acid (H₂CO₃). Na⁺ does not hydrolyse, but the carbonate ion does: CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻. The OH⁻ ions produced make [OH⁻] > [H⁺], so the solution is basic (pH > 7).
keyPoints: Salt of strong base + weak acid

text: Define oxidising agent and reducing agent. Identify both in: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.
modelAnswer: An oxidising agent accepts electrons (its O.N. decreases) and is itself reduced. A reducing agent donates electrons (its O.N. increases) and is itself oxidised. In 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, Na goes 0 → +1 (oxidised), so Na is the reducing agent. Cl goes 0 → −1 (reduced), so Cl₂ is the oxidising agent.

text: Balance the following equation by the ion-electron (half-reaction) method in acidic medium: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + Fe²⁺ → Cr³⁺ + Fe³⁺.
modelAnswer:
Oxidation half: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ (× 6).
Reduction half: Cr₂O₇²⁻ → 2Cr³⁺. Balance O with water: Cr₂O₇²⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O. Balance H with H⁺: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O. Balance charge with electrons: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O.
Add, cancelling the 6e⁻: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6Fe²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O. Check: charge on the left = −2 + 14 + 12 = +24; on the right = +6 + 18 = +24. Balanced.
keyPoints: Balance O with H₂O and H with H⁺

text: Balance by the oxidation-number method: MnO₄⁻ + I⁻ → MnO₂ + I₂ (basic medium).
modelAnswer:
O.N. changes: Mn +7 → +4 (gains 3 e⁻); I −1 → 0 (loses 1 e⁻ per I, 2 e⁻ per I₂).
LCM of 3 and 2 = 6: 2MnO₄⁻ + 6I⁻ → 2MnO₂ + 3I₂.
Charge: left = −8, right = 0. In basic medium add 8OH⁻ to the right: 2MnO₄⁻ + 6I⁻ → 2MnO₂ + 3I₂ + 8OH⁻.
Balance H and O with water on the left: 2MnO₄⁻ + 6I⁻ + 4H₂O → 2MnO₂ + 3I₂ + 8OH⁻. (O: 8 + 4 = 12 = 4 + 8 ✓; H: 8 = 8 ✓)
keyPoints: Balance charge with OH⁻ in basic medium

text: State any four rules used for assigning oxidation numbers.
modelAnswer: (i) An element in its free (uncombined) state has O.N. 0 (e.g. Na, O₂, P₄). (ii) For a monatomic ion, O.N. = its charge. (iii) Oxygen is usually −2, except in peroxides (−1), superoxides (−½) and OF₂ (+2). (iv) Hydrogen is +1 with non-metals and −1 in metal hydrides (NaH). (v) Fluorine is always −1. (vi) The sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral compound is 0 and in an ion equals its charge.

text: (a) What is an electrochemical series? Give any three of its applications. (b) Given E°: Ag⁺/Ag = +0.80 V, Zn²⁺/Zn = −0.76 V, Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V. Predict, with reasons, whether (i) Zn will displace Cu from CuSO₄ solution and (ii) Cu will displace Ag from AgNO₃ solution and (iii) Ag will liberate H₂ from dilute HCl. Calculate E°cell for the cell in which Zn reduces Ag⁺.
modelAnswer:
(a) The electrochemical series is the arrangement of electrodes (half-cells) in order of their standard reduction potentials. Applications: (1) comparing the relative strengths of oxidising and reducing agents; (2) predicting whether a metal will displace another metal, or hydrogen from acids; (3) calculating the emf of a cell and predicting whether a redox reaction is feasible (E°cell > 0).
(b) (i) Yes. Zn (−0.76 V) has a lower reduction potential than Cu (+0.34 V), so it is the stronger reducing agent and reduces Cu²⁺: E° = 0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V > 0.
(ii) Yes. Cu (+0.34) is below Ag (+0.80) in the series: E° = 0.80 − 0.34 = +0.46 V > 0.
(iii) No. E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V is greater than 0 V (SHE), so Ag cannot reduce H⁺: E° = 0 − 0.80 = −0.80 V < 0.
Zn–Ag cell: E°cell = 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V.

text: Why is hydrogen given a unique position in the periodic table? Give one resemblance with alkali metals and one with halogens.
modelAnswer: Hydrogen resembles both alkali metals and halogens but differs from each, so it is placed separately (usually at the top of Group 1). With the alkali metals: it has one valence electron (1s¹) and forms H⁺ (it is +1 in HCl, H₂O). With the halogens: it needs only one electron to complete its shell (like F and Cl), forms H⁻ in metal hydrides (NaH) and exists as diatomic H₂.

text: What causes temporary and permanent hardness of water? Give one method each to remove them, with equations.
modelAnswer:
Temporary hardness is due to the bicarbonates of Ca and Mg. It is removed by boiling: Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃↓ + H₂O + CO₂ and Mg(HCO₃)₂ → Mg(OH)₂↓ + 2CO₂. It can also be removed by Clark's method: Ca(HCO₃)₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → 2CaCO₃↓ + 2H₂O.
Permanent hardness is due to the chlorides and sulphates of Ca and Mg. It is removed by washing soda: CaCl₂ + Na₂CO₃ → CaCO₃↓ + 2NaCl, or by the ion-exchange (zeolite) method: 2NaZ + Ca²⁺ → CaZ₂ + 2Na⁺ (or by Calgon).
keyPoints: Boiling or Clark's method with equation
Washing soda / ion exchange with equation

text: Write equations to show that hydrogen peroxide acts as (a) an oxidising agent in acidic medium and (b) a reducing agent in acidic medium. Why does it have this dual nature?
modelAnswer:
(a) As an oxidising agent: 2Fe²⁺ + 2H⁺ + H₂O₂ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2H₂O (or PbS + 4H₂O₂ → PbSO₄ + 4H₂O).
(b) As a reducing agent: 2MnO₄⁻ + 6H⁺ + 5H₂O₂ → 2Mn²⁺ + 8H₂O + 5O₂.
Dual nature: the oxygen in H₂O₂ is in the −1 oxidation state, which lies between −2 (in H₂O) and 0 (in O₂). So it can be reduced to −2 or oxidised to 0, depending on the other reactant.

text: What is heavy water? Give two of its uses.
modelAnswer: Heavy water is deuterium oxide, D₂O, in which both hydrogen atoms are the heavier isotope deuterium (²H). Uses: (i) as a moderator in nuclear reactors, to slow down fast neutrons; (ii) as a tracer for studying reaction mechanisms; (iii) to prepare other deuterium compounds, e.g. CaC₂ + 2D₂O → C₂D₂ + Ca(OD)₂.

text: (a) Describe the laboratory preparation of H₂O₂ from barium peroxide. (b) Explain the structure of H₂O₂ with the approximate dihedral angle in the gas phase. (c) What is meant by '10 volume' H₂O₂? Calculate its strength in g L⁻¹ and its molarity. (d) Mention two uses of H₂O₂.
modelAnswer:
(a) Hydrated barium peroxide is treated with ice-cold dilute sulphuric acid: BaO₂·8H₂O + H₂SO₄ → BaSO₄↓ + H₂O₂ + 8H₂O. The insoluble BaSO₄ is filtered off, leaving a dilute H₂O₂ solution.
(b) H₂O₂ has a non-planar 'open book' structure. The O–O bond lies along the spine and the two O–H bonds lie in planes inclined at a dihedral angle of about 111.5° in the gas phase (about 90° in the crystal).
(c) '10 volume' means 1 L of the solution gives 10 L of O₂ at STP on decomposition. 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂: 68 g of H₂O₂ gives 22.4 L of O₂. So 10 L comes from 68 × 10/22.4 = 30.36 g, giving a strength of 30.36 g L⁻¹ (≈ 3% w/v). Molarity = 30.36/34 = 0.893 M.
(d) Uses: bleaching of textiles, paper pulp and hair; as a mild antiseptic (perhydrol); in environmental (green) chemistry to treat effluents; as an oxidiser in rocket fuels.

text: What is the diagonal relationship? Give two similarities between Li and Mg.
modelAnswer: The diagonal relationship is the similarity between an element of period 2 and the element diagonally below and to its right in period 3 (Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si). It arises from their similar polarising power (charge/size ratio). Li–Mg similarities: (i) both burn in N₂ to form nitrides (Li₃N, Mg₃N₂); (ii) their carbonates decompose on heating to give the oxide and CO₂; (iii) both form only normal oxides (Li₂O, MgO); (iv) their chlorides are deliquescent and soluble in ethanol.

text: Explain the anomalous behaviour of lithium compared with the other alkali metals. Give any three points of difference.
modelAnswer:
Lithium is anomalous because of its very small atomic and ionic size, its high polarising power, its relatively high IE and electronegativity, and the absence of d-orbitals.
Differences: (i) Li is much harder and has higher melting and boiling points. (ii) Li forms the normal oxide Li₂O on burning, while Na forms a peroxide and K a superoxide. (iii) Li reacts directly with N₂ to form Li₃N; the others do not. (iv) Li₂CO₃ and LiNO₃ decompose on heating (4LiNO₃ → 2Li₂O + 4NO₂ + O₂), while NaNO₃ gives NaNO₂ + O₂. (v) LiCl is deliquescent and partly covalent, soluble in organic solvents.
keyPoints: Reasons: small size, high polarising power

text: Describe the Solvay process for the manufacture of sodium carbonate, with equations.
modelAnswer:
Brine saturated with ammonia is treated with CO₂:
NH₃ + H₂O + CO₂ → NH₄HCO₃
NaCl + NH₄HCO₃ → NaHCO₃↓ + NH₄Cl
The sparingly soluble NaHCO₃ crystallises out. It is filtered and heated (calcined): 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂. The CO₂ is recycled.
NH₃ is recovered by heating the NH₄Cl with Ca(OH)₂ (from limestone): 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → 2NH₃ + CaCl₂ + 2H₂O. CaCl₂ is the only by-product.

text: What happens when (a) plaster of Paris is mixed with water and (b) slaked lime is treated with chlorine? Write equations.
modelAnswer:
(a) Plaster of Paris absorbs water and sets into a hard mass of gypsum: CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O → CaSO₄·2H₂O.
(b) Bleaching powder is formed: 2Ca(OH)₂ + 2Cl₂ → CaCl₂ + Ca(OCl)₂ + 2H₂O. (Simplified: Ca(OH)₂ + Cl₂ → CaOCl₂ + H₂O.)
keyPoints: POP sets to gypsum with equation

text: (a) Discuss the trends in solubility of hydroxides and sulphates of Group 2 elements and explain them in terms of lattice and hydration enthalpies. (b) Give the biological importance of Na, K, Mg and Ca. (c) 16.8 g of sodium hydrogencarbonate is heated strongly. Calculate the volume of CO₂ evolved at STP.
modelAnswer:
(a) Solubility depends on the balance between lattice enthalpy (which opposes dissolution) and hydration enthalpy (which favours it). For hydroxides, lattice enthalpy falls faster than hydration enthalpy as the cation grows, so solubility increases from Be(OH)₂ to Ba(OH)₂. For sulphates, the large SO₄²⁻ ion means lattice enthalpy hardly changes, while hydration enthalpy falls sharply with cation size, so solubility decreases from BeSO₄ (soluble) to BaSO₄ (insoluble).
(b) Na⁺: the main extracellular cation; controls fluid balance and nerve signal transmission. K⁺: the main intracellular cation; activates enzymes, helps oxidise glucose to make ATP and works with Na⁺ in the Na⁺–K⁺ pump. Mg²⁺: in chlorophyll; a cofactor for enzymes that use ATP. Ca²⁺: in bones and teeth (as apatite); needed for blood clotting, muscle contraction and heartbeat regulation.
(c) 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂. n(NaHCO₃) = 16.8/84 = 0.2 mol, so n(CO₂) = 0.1 mol. V = 0.1 × 22.4 = 2.24 L at STP.
keyPoints: Hydroxide solubility ↑ down group with reason
Sulphate solubility ↓ down group with reason
Role of Na, K, Mg, Ca

text: Explain why boron trifluoride behaves as a Lewis acid.
modelAnswer: In BF₃ boron has only six electrons in its valence shell (an incomplete octet) and a vacant 2p orbital. It can therefore accept a lone pair from an electron-pair donor such as NH₃ or F⁻, forming adducts like F₃B←NH₃ or [BF₄]⁻. An electron-pair acceptor is a Lewis acid.
keyPoints: Incomplete octet / empty p orbital on B

text: Describe the structure of diborane with a labelled description. How is it prepared, and what happens when it burns in air?
modelAnswer:
Structure: the two B atoms and four terminal H atoms lie in one plane. Two bridging H atoms sit above and below this plane. Each B is roughly sp³ hybridised. There are four normal 2-centre–2-electron terminal B–H bonds and two 3-centre–2-electron B–H–B bridge (banana) bonds. The bridge bonds are longer than the terminal ones.
Preparation: 4BF₃ + 3LiAlH₄ → 2B₂H₆ + 3LiF + 3AlF₃ (in ether), or 2NaBH₄ + I₂ → B₂H₆ + 2NaI + H₂ in the laboratory.
Combustion: B₂H₆ + 3O₂ → B₂O₃ + 3H₂O, which is highly exothermic.

text: Compare the structures and properties of diamond and graphite.
modelAnswer:
Diamond: each C is sp³ hybridised and covalently bonded to four others in a rigid 3D tetrahedral network (C–C 154 pm). It is extremely hard, has a very high melting point, is an electrical insulator and is transparent. It is used in cutting tools and jewellery.
Graphite: each C is sp² hybridised and bonded to three others in flat hexagonal layers (C–C 141.5 pm). The layers are held by weak van der Waals forces (340 pm apart). The fourth electron is delocalised, so graphite conducts electricity. The layers slide over each other, making it soft and slippery, so it is used as a lubricant and in electrodes.
keyPoints: Graphite sp², layers, van der Waals between layers

text: What is the inert pair effect? Illustrate it with an example from Group 13 or Group 14.
modelAnswer: The inert pair effect is the reluctance of the ns² electrons of the heavier p-block elements to take part in bonding. It arises from poor shielding by the intervening d and f electrons. As a result, the oxidation state two units below the group oxidation state becomes more stable down the group. Example: in Group 13 thallium is more stable as Tl⁺ than Tl³⁺; in Group 14 lead is more stable as Pb²⁺ than Pb⁴⁺ (so PbO₂ is a strong oxidising agent).
keyPoints: Due to poor shielding by d/f electrons

text: (a) What are silicones? How are they prepared? Explain the roles of R₃SiCl, R₂SiCl₂ and RSiCl₃. (b) Give two properties and two uses of silicones. (c) What are zeolites? Mention one important use.
modelAnswer:
(a) Silicones are synthetic organosilicon polymers with the repeating unit –(R₂SiO)–, i.e. an –Si–O–Si– backbone with alkyl or aryl groups on silicon. Preparation: alkyl chlorosilanes are made by heating RCl with Si using a Cu catalyst (Rochow process), e.g. 2CH₃Cl + Si → (CH₃)₂SiCl₂. Hydrolysis gives silanols: (CH₃)₂SiCl₂ + 2H₂O → (CH₃)₂Si(OH)₂ + 2HCl. These condense, losing water, to form –[(CH₃)₂SiO]ₙ– chains.
Roles: R₂SiCl₂ (two –OH groups) builds linear chains; RSiCl₃ (three –OH groups) produces cross-linked 3D silicones; R₃SiCl (one –OH) caps the chain ends and controls the chain length.
(b) Properties: water-repellent (hydrophobic), thermally stable, chemically inert, good electrical insulators, and non-toxic. Uses: sealants and greases, electrical insulation, water-proofing fabrics, and surgical and cosmetic implants.
(c) Zeolites are 3D aluminosilicates in which some Si⁴⁺ is replaced by Al³⁺, with the extra negative charge balanced by cations such as Na⁺. They have honeycomb-like pores. Uses: as shape-selective catalysts (ZSM-5 converts alcohols to gasoline) and for water softening (ion exchange).

text: Why is boric acid considered a Lewis acid? Write the equation for its ionisation in water.
modelAnswer: Boron in B(OH)₃ is electron-deficient (it has only six valence electrons). It does not release a proton directly. Instead, it accepts a hydroxide ion (an electron pair) from water, releasing an H⁺ from the water molecule: B(OH)₃ + 2H₂O ⇌ [B(OH)₄]⁻ + H₃O⁺. So it acts as a weak monobasic Lewis acid (pKₐ ≈ 9.2).

chapter: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
text: What are electrophiles and nucleophiles? Give two examples of each.
modelAnswer: Electrophiles are electron-deficient species ('electron lovers') that attack regions of high electron density. They may be positive or neutral with an empty orbital: H⁺, NO₂⁺, Cl⁺, BF₃, AlCl₃, carbocations. Nucleophiles are electron-rich species ('nucleus lovers') that donate an electron pair to an electron-deficient centre: OH⁻, CN⁻, Cl⁻, NH₃, H₂O, ROH.

chapter: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
text: Explain the inductive effect with an example. How does it account for the order of acidity: Cl₃CCOOH > Cl₂CHCOOH > ClCH₂COOH > CH₃COOH?
modelAnswer:
The inductive effect is the permanent shift of σ-electron density along a carbon chain, caused by an electronegative (−I) or electron-releasing (+I) atom or group. It weakens rapidly with distance. Example: in CH₃CH₂Cl, the Cl pulls electrons, leaving partial positive charges on C-1 (largest) and C-2.
Cl is a −I group. It withdraws electron density from the –COO⁻ group, spreading out the negative charge and stabilising the carboxylate anion, which makes it easier to lose H⁺. More Cl atoms give a stronger combined −I effect, so trichloroacetic acid is the strongest and acetic acid (CH₃ is +I) is the weakest.

chapter: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
text: Describe Lassaigne's test for nitrogen, sulphur and halogens in an organic compound, with equations.
modelAnswer:
The compound is fused with sodium metal, and the fused mass is extracted with water (the sodium fusion extract).
Nitrogen: Na + C + N → NaCN. The extract is boiled with FeSO₄ and acidified with H₂SO₄ (with Fe³⁺ present): 6CN⁻ + Fe²⁺ → [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻; 3[Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ + 4Fe³⁺ → Fe₄[Fe(CN)₆]₃, Prussian blue.
Sulphur: 2Na + S → Na₂S. With sodium nitroprusside, S²⁻ + [Fe(CN)₅NO]²⁻ → [Fe(CN)₅NOS]⁴⁻, a violet colour. (Or a black PbS precipitate with lead acetate.)
Halogens: Na + X → NaX. The extract is boiled with HNO₃, then AgNO₃ is added: X⁻ + Ag⁺ → AgX. A white precipitate soluble in NH₃ means Cl; pale yellow, sparingly soluble means Br; yellow, insoluble means I.
keyPoints: Sodium fusion converts covalent N, S, X into ionic NaCN, Na₂S, NaX
AgX precipitates for halogens after HNO₃

chapter: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
text: (a) Explain the principle of Dumas' method for estimating nitrogen. (b) 0.30 g of an organic compound gave 50 mL of nitrogen collected over water at 300 K and 715 mm Hg pressure. The aqueous tension at 300 K is 15 mm Hg. Calculate the percentage of nitrogen in the compound. (c) Why is Kjeldahl's method not used for nitrobenzene?
modelAnswer:
(a) A known mass of the compound is heated with copper(II) oxide in an atmosphere of CO₂. Carbon and hydrogen are oxidised to CO₂ and H₂O, and nitrogen is set free as N₂ (any oxides of nitrogen are reduced to N₂ over hot copper gauze). The gases are passed into KOH solution, which absorbs CO₂, and the N₂ is collected and its volume measured.
(b) Pressure of dry N₂ = 715 − 15 = 700 mm Hg.
Volume at STP: V₀ = (700 × 50 × 273) ÷ (760 × 300) = 41.9 mL.
22 400 mL of N₂ at STP has a mass of 28 g, so 41.9 mL has a mass of 28 × 41.9/22 400 = 0.0524 g.
% N = 0.0524/0.30 × 100 = 17.5%.
(c) In nitrobenzene the nitrogen is in a nitro group. It is not converted into ammonium sulphate when heated with concentrated H₂SO₄, so Kjeldahl's method would give a wrong (low) result.
keyPoints: Principle: N → N₂ with CuO, CO₂ absorbed by KOH

chapter: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
text: Distinguish between a carbocation and a carbanion with respect to charge, hybridisation and shape.
modelAnswer:
Carbocation: carbon with a positive charge and only six electrons in its valence shell. It is sp² hybridised and trigonal planar, with an empty p orbital. It is stabilised by +I and hyperconjugation (3° > 2° > 1°).
Carbanion: carbon with a negative charge and an unshared pair (eight electrons). It is sp³ hybridised and pyramidal. It is stabilised by −I groups (stability methyl > 1° > 2° > 3°).

chapter: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
text: What is hyperconjugation? Use it to explain why propene is more stable than ethene.
modelAnswer: Hyperconjugation is the delocalisation of σ electrons of a C–H bond on a carbon next to (α to) an unsaturated system or a positive carbon into an adjacent empty or partly filled p orbital or π orbital. It is also called 'no-bond resonance'. Propene (CH₃–CH=CH₂) has 3 α-hydrogens that can take part in hyperconjugation with the π bond, which spreads out the electron density and stabilises the molecule. Ethene has no α-hydrogens. So propene is more stable (it has a lower heat of hydrogenation).
keyPoints: Definition: σ(C–H) delocalisation into adjacent π/p

text: State Markovnikov's rule. Write the product of the addition of HBr to propene in the absence and presence of peroxide.
modelAnswer: Markovnikov's rule: when an unsymmetrical reagent HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the negative part (X) attaches to the carbon of the double bond that carries fewer hydrogen atoms. Without peroxide: CH₃CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CHBrCH₃ (2-bromopropane). With peroxide (Kharasch, anti-Markovnikov): CH₃CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH₂CH₂Br (1-bromopropane).

text: Explain the free-radical mechanism of the chlorination of methane in the presence of sunlight.
modelAnswer:
Initiation: Cl–Cl → (hν) 2Cl·, homolytic fission of chlorine.
Propagation: Cl· + CH₄ → CH₃· + HCl; then CH₃· + Cl–Cl → CH₃Cl + Cl·. The regenerated Cl· continues the chain. Further substitution gives CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄.
Termination: radicals combine: Cl· + Cl· → Cl₂; CH₃· + CH₃· → C₂H₆; CH₃· + Cl· → CH₃Cl. Traces of ethane in the product support this mechanism.
keyPoints: Initiation by homolysis of Cl₂ in light

text: Draw Newman projections of the staggered and eclipsed conformations of ethane and explain which is more stable.
modelAnswer:
In a Newman projection the molecule is viewed along the C–C bond. The front carbon is a point with three C–H bonds at 120°, and the rear carbon is a circle with its three C–H bonds.
Staggered: the rear C–H bonds lie exactly between the front ones (dihedral angle 60°).
Eclipsed: the rear C–H bonds lie directly behind the front ones (dihedral angle 0°).
The staggered form is more stable because the bonding electron pairs are as far apart as possible, so there is minimum repulsion (torsional strain). The energy difference is only about 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹, so the two forms interconvert rapidly at room temperature and cannot be separated.
keyPoints: Staggered more stable — minimum torsional strain

text: (a) What is aromaticity? State Hückel's rule and classify benzene, cyclobutadiene and the cyclopentadienyl anion. (b) Explain the mechanism of electrophilic substitution in benzene using nitration as an example. (c) Explain why –OH is ortho/para-directing while –NO₂ is meta-directing.
modelAnswer:
(a) Aromaticity is the special stability of certain cyclic, planar, fully conjugated molecules with delocalised π electrons. Hückel's rule: such a system is aromatic if it has (4n + 2) π electrons (n = 0, 1, 2 …). Benzene has 6 π electrons, so it is aromatic. Cyclobutadiene has 4 π electrons (4n), so it is antiaromatic. The cyclopentadienyl anion has 6 π electrons, so it is aromatic.
(b) Step 1, generating the electrophile: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻. Step 2: NO₂⁺ attacks the π cloud, forming a resonance-stabilised carbocation (the σ-complex, or arenium ion). The carbon under attack becomes sp³ and aromaticity is temporarily lost. This step is slow. Step 3: HSO₄⁻ removes the H⁺ from the sp³ carbon, restoring aromaticity and giving nitrobenzene.
(c) –OH donates a lone pair into the ring (+R effect), increasing the electron density mainly at the ortho and para positions (as resonance structures show). This activates the ring and directs electrophiles there. –NO₂ withdraws electrons (−R, −I), reducing the electron density most at the ortho and para positions. The meta position is relatively less depleted, so substitution occurs at meta and the ring is deactivated.
keyPoints: Resonance explanation of o/p vs m direction

text: How will you convert (a) ethyne to benzene and (b) sodium acetate to methane? Write equations.
modelAnswer:
(a) Ethyne is passed through a red-hot iron tube at about 873 K (cyclic polymerisation): 3HC≡CH → C₆H₆.
(b) Sodium acetate is heated with soda lime (NaOH + CaO) (decarboxylation): CH₃COONa + NaOH → (CaO, Δ) CH₄ + Na₂CO₃.

text: Why does benzene undergo substitution rather than addition reactions, although it is highly unsaturated?
modelAnswer: Benzene's six π electrons are delocalised over the ring, which gives it a large resonance (aromatic) stabilisation energy of about 150 kJ mol⁻¹. Addition would destroy this delocalised system and the extra stability. In substitution an H is replaced while the aromatic sextet is kept, so the product is still aromatic. Hence benzene prefers electrophilic substitution and adds only under drastic conditions (e.g. H₂/Ni at high T, Cl₂ in UV).

text: What is acid rain? Name the main gases responsible and give one harmful effect.
modelAnswer: Acid rain is rainwater with a pH below 5.6. It forms when oxides of sulphur and nitrogen (SO₂, NO₂) react with water and oxygen in the air to form H₂SO₄ and HNO₃: 2SO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 2H₂SO₄; 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃. Harmful effects: it corrodes buildings and monuments made of marble or limestone (e.g. the Taj Mahal), damages leaves and forests, acidifies lakes (killing fish) and leaches nutrients from soil.

text: Differentiate between classical smog and photochemical smog.
modelAnswer:
Classical (London) smog: smoke + fog + SO₂. It forms in cool, humid climates. It is chemically reducing. It comes mainly from burning coal. It causes bronchitis and other breathing problems.
Photochemical (Los Angeles) smog: forms in warm, dry, sunny climates. NOₓ and hydrocarbons from vehicle exhaust react under sunlight to give O₃, PAN, formaldehyde and acrolein. It is chemically oxidising. It causes eye irritation, damage to rubber and plants, and breathing problems.

text: Explain, with equations, how chlorofluorocarbons deplete the ozone layer.
modelAnswer:
CFCs are inert in the lower atmosphere, so they drift up into the stratosphere. There, UV light breaks them down: CF₂Cl₂ → (UV) ·CF₂Cl + Cl·.
The chlorine radical destroys ozone: Cl· + O₃ → ClO· + O₂. Then ClO· + O → Cl· + O₂.
The Cl· radical is regenerated, so this is a chain reaction in which one Cl atom can destroy thousands of O₃ molecules. In polar regions, polar stratospheric clouds also convert ClONO₂ and HCl into Cl₂ and HOCl, which are photolysed in spring to give Cl·. This produces the ozone hole. As a result more UV reaches Earth, causing skin cancer, cataracts and harm to crops and plankton.

text: What is green chemistry? Give two examples of its application.
modelAnswer: Green chemistry is the design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use and production of hazardous substances. It uses safer solvents, less energy, renewable feedstocks and less waste. Examples: (i) dry cleaning with liquid CO₂ instead of tetrachloroethene; (ii) bleaching paper with H₂O₂ instead of chlorine; (iii) making ethanal from ethene in water with a Pd(II)/Cu(II) catalyst.
keyPoints: Definition: minimise hazardous substances and waste

text: (a) What is the greenhouse effect? Name four greenhouse gases. (b) Explain how an increase in greenhouse gases leads to global warming and list three likely consequences. (c) Define BOD and explain why a high BOD indicates polluted water. (d) Suggest two measures to control soil pollution.
modelAnswer:
(a) The greenhouse effect is the trapping of heat near Earth's surface by gases that let in sunlight but absorb the infrared radiation re-emitted by the surface and radiate part of it back. Greenhouse gases: CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, water vapour, CFCs, O₃.
(b) Burning fossil fuels, deforestation, agriculture and landfills increase the concentrations of these gases, so more IR is trapped and the average global temperature rises (global warming). Consequences: melting of polar ice and glaciers, and rising sea levels; more extreme weather and changing rainfall; spread of diseases such as malaria; harm to crops and ecosystems.
(c) BOD is the amount of oxygen (in ppm) needed by micro-organisms to break down the organic matter in a given volume of water (usually measured over 5 days at 20 °C). Polluted water contains a lot of organic waste, so microbes use more O₂, giving a high BOD. This lowers dissolved oxygen and harms aquatic life. Clean water has BOD < 5 ppm.
(d) Reduce the use of chemical fertilisers and persistent pesticides (use biofertilisers and biopesticides); dispose of and recycle industrial and domestic solid waste properly; prevent soil erosion by afforestation; treat industrial effluents before discharge.
